messages.subject: zero-inflated models and DSM
parts:
Hi,
I'm fitting some models to cetacean line transect data using dsm in R, and I have one data set in particular that is causing me problems. It has a high percentage of zeros (~89%) and remains overdispersed even when using negative binomial or tweedie distributions. I've tried running it with only a s(X,Y) and also with additional environmental covariates. I would ideally like to perform a zero-inflated Poisson model, but I cannot figure out how to do this in DSM. Any suggestions are greatly appreciated. It also has a corARMA(p=1,q=0) correlation structure, so I've been running it as a negbin GAMM, but the density predictions from the negbin model do not look realistic, so looking for other modelling alternatives, and the ZIP seems like the next logical progression.

I also have a second question about the theta parameter in the negbin GAMM in dsm - it has to be specified by the user, and it appears only one value can be given. When I've tried entering a range of values, e.g. theta=c(0.01,0.5), R throws a warning message saying that only the first value has been used. So I'm looking for some advice about how to choose an appropriate theta. The choice of this value appears to affect the abundance estimate from my model a great deal, which worries me.

Thanks,
- Brianna

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] zero-inflated models and DSM
parts:
Hi Brianna, hi listfolks,

We've not investigated using these zero-inflated distributions in dsm
yet and I don't know how well they are supported in the current
framework. Your best bet would be to use dsm to create the dataset, then
extract the $data column from the resulting model, then pass that back
to gam() to get started with ZIP.

That being said, I wonder what you are using to work out if the model is
working well. In general plots of observed vs. predicted per segment
will look bad because of the way that the smooths smudge out the
density. dsm provides obs_exp() which lets you compare the observed vs
expected over binned versions of the covariates (in the dsm or detection
function). So, for example, looking at obs vs. expected for different
Beaufort levels or bathymetric depth intervals may reveal the model is
doing well, once aggregated. An example output is given in
https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.07996 (see tables 3 and 4).

As it says in the mgcv::negbin manual page: "'gamm' does not support
'theta' estimation". There are a few options, one of which would be to
use a value of theta derived from a gam() fit to the same data using the
nb() response.

With both of these approaches (GAMM and ZIP) are starting to get fairly
complicated models with additional assumptions and additional fitting
headaches. The fitting for gamm() is notoriously tricky, and I've had
very limited success fitting such models on datasets I've encountered --
the additional complexity rarely seems to pay off. For the ZIP, you'll
need to specify a for the presences separately to the abundance. Making
the separation between those two parts of the model, and which goes in
which, involves some assumptions about how the system works.

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave
